questions.stem: Why do cells need a supply of amino acids?
options: To form the phospholipid bilayer that surrounds the cytoplasm
To build proteins, including enzymes and membrane proteins
To release energy directly by combining with oxygen in respiration
To absorb light energy for the production of glucose in the cell
questions.explanation: Amino acids are the monomers joined by ribosomes to make proteins, such as enzymes, channels and structural proteins. The bilayer is made of phospholipids, and light is absorbed by chlorophyll.

questions.stem: What is the main role of glucose in cells?
options: It is the pigment that absorbs light energy in plant chloroplasts
It is broken down in cellular respiration to release energy as ATP
It carries oxygen from the lungs to cells all around the body
It is joined to other glucose molecules to make DNA in the nucleus
questions.explanation: Glucose is the main respiratory substrate; its chemical energy is transferred to ATP. Oxygen is carried by haemoglobin, and DNA is built from nucleotides, not glucose.

questions.stem: A plant grown in soil lacking magnesium ions develops yellow leaves. What best explains this?
options: Magnesium is the main source of energy for the plant's growing leaf cells
Magnesium carries water up the xylem, so the leaves are short of water
Magnesium is needed to make cellulose, so the leaves lose their green walls
Magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule, so less chlorophyll is made
questions.explanation: Each chlorophyll molecule contains a magnesium ion at its centre, so a shortage reduces chlorophyll and leaves turn yellow (chlorosis). Cell walls are not green; the colour comes from chlorophyll in chloroplasts.

questions.stem: Why does a person with too little iron in their diet often feel tired and short of breath?
options: Iron is the main fuel for cellular respiration, so less energy is released
Iron forms the walls of the alveoli, so less air can enter the lungs each breath
Iron is needed to make glucose in the liver, so blood sugar levels fall
Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches cells for respiration
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells contains iron and carries oxygen. With less haemoglobin, less oxygen is delivered, aerobic respiration slows and the person tires easily.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a cell requirement and its role is correct?
options: Sodium ions: the source of energy for the cell's protein synthesis
Water: the solvent in which the cell's chemical reactions take place
Oxygen: the raw material from which cells build their amino acids
Carbon dioxide: the gas that animal cells need for aerobic respiration
questions.explanation: Water dissolves the substances in cytoplasm, so reactions happen in solution, and it is also a reactant in photosynthesis. Animal cells need oxygen for respiration and release carbon dioxide as a waste.

questions.stem: Plants absorb nitrate ions from the soil. What do they use the nitrogen for?
options: Making cellulose, which strengthens the plant cell walls
Making oxygen, which is released from the leaves at night
Making amino acids, which are built into proteins
Making glucose, which is stored in the roots as starch
questions.explanation: Amino acids contain nitrogen, so plants need nitrate to make them and then their proteins. Glucose, starch and cellulose contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.stem: For which cells is carbon dioxide a requirement and not only a waste product?
options: Photosynthesising cells, such as leaf palisade cells
Muscle cells, which respire rapidly during exercise
Red blood cells, which carry gases around the body
Bacterial cells, which divide quickly by binary fission
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a reactant in photosynthesis, so chloroplast-containing cells need it. Muscle cells produce CO₂ in respiration and must get rid of it.

questions.stem: Which are the reactants of aerobic cellular respiration?
options: Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and water
Glucose and carbon dioxide
Oxygen and water
questions.explanation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy, so glucose and oxygen react and carbon dioxide and water are produced. Carbon dioxide and water are the reactants of photosynthesis.

questions.stem: In which organelle do the aerobic stages of cellular respiration take place in eukaryotic cells?
options: Mitochondria
Chloroplasts
Ribosomes
Lysosomes
questions.explanation: Most of the energy from glucose is released in the mitochondria, which need oxygen. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, not respiration.

questions.stem: In the respiration equation, glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy, what happens to the energy released?
options: It is used to turn carbon dioxide back into oxygen inside the mitochondria
Some is captured in ATP for cell processes, and the rest is lost as heat
All of it is stored as new glucose molecules for later use by the cell
All of it is released as light, which the cell uses to make chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Respiration transfers part of the chemical energy in glucose to ATP, which powers active transport, synthesis and movement; the rest is released as heat. Respiration does not make glucose or oxygen.

questions.stem: According to the summary equation, how many molecules of oxygen are needed to fully respire 3 molecules of glucose?
questions.explanation: Each glucose needs 6 O₂ (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O), so 3 glucose molecules need 3 × 6 = 18 O₂. Six is the number for a single glucose molecule, and 12 is the number for two.

questions.stem: According to the summary equation, how many molecules of water are produced when 2 molecules of glucose are fully respired?
questions.explanation: One glucose gives 6 H₂O, so 2 glucose give 2 × 6 = 12 H₂O. The same reasoning gives 12 CO₂ from 2 glucose.

questions.stem: A student says photosynthesis and respiration are exact reverses of each other. Which is the best evaluation?
options: The claim is wrong, because photosynthesis produces carbon dioxide while respiration uses it up
The claim is wrong, because only animal cells respire while only plant cells carry out photosynthesis
The summary equations are reversed, but the processes use different pathways, organelles and enzymes
The claim is fully correct, because both processes happen in the same organelle in the reverse order
questions.explanation: The reactants of one are the products of the other, but photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts using light energy, while respiration happens largely in mitochondria and releases energy as ATP, each through many enzyme-controlled steps. Plant cells respire too.

questions.stem: In the photosynthesis equation, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, what is written above the arrow?
options: Heat and water
Light and chlorophyll
Oxygen and ATP
Glucose and enzymes
questions.explanation: Light provides the energy and chlorophyll absorbs it, so both are written above the arrow as conditions rather than reactants. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, not a condition.

questions.stem: What is the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
options: It absorbs light energy that drives the reaction
It supplies the carbon atoms that make up glucose
It releases oxygen by breaking down glucose
It stores the glucose made in the chloroplast
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is a pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs mainly red and blue light. The carbon in glucose comes from carbon dioxide, not chlorophyll.

questions.stem: Which energy transformation does photosynthesis carry out?
options: Chemical energy in glucose to light energy
Heat energy to chemical energy stored in oxygen gas
Chemical energy in ATP to heat energy in water
Light energy to chemical energy stored in glucose
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis captures light energy and stores it in the bonds of glucose. Respiration later releases that chemical energy, transferring part of it to ATP.

questions.stem: Leaves are placed in three tubes of red hydrogencarbonate indicator: tube 1 in bright light, tube 2 wrapped in foil, tube 3 with no leaf in bright light. After 2 hours tube 1 is purple, tube 2 is yellow and tube 3 is red. What do the results show?
options: In light, photosynthesis removed more CO₂ than respiration added; in the dark, respiration added CO₂
In light, respiration stopped completely; in the dark, photosynthesis added CO₂ to the indicator
In light, the leaf released CO₂ by photosynthesis; in the dark, the leaf absorbed CO₂ by respiration
The light changed the indicator colour directly, because the tube without a leaf turned purple too
questions.explanation: Purple means CO₂ fell, yellow means CO₂ rose, and red means no change. In light, photosynthesis outpaced respiration; in the dark only respiration occurred. Tube 3 is the control, showing light alone does not change the colour.

questions.stem: When does a green plant carry out cellular respiration?
options: All the time, in both light and darkness
Only at night, when photosynthesis stops
Only during the day, when glucose is made
Never, because plants make their own glucose
questions.explanation: All living cells respire continuously to supply ATP. During the day a plant's photosynthesis is usually faster than its respiration, so the respiration is masked, but it still happens.

questions.stem: What is an enzyme?
options: A lipid that stores energy for reactions until it is needed
A protein that is used up as it supplies energy to a reaction
A carbohydrate that forms the substrate of most of the cell's reactions
A protein that speeds up a specific reaction and is not used up
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts, almost all proteins, that increase the rate of particular reactions and can be used again. They do not supply energy; they lower the energy needed to start the reaction.

questions.stem: What is the active site of an enzyme?
options: The gene on a chromosome that codes for the enzyme
The organelle inside the cell where the enzyme is made
The region with a specific shape where the substrate binds
The part of the enzyme that is released as the product
questions.explanation: The active site is a pocket formed by the enzyme's folded chain of amino acids, shaped to bind its substrate. The enzyme itself is not part of the product.

questions.stem: How does an enzyme increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It lowers the activation energy needed for the reaction to start
It raises the temperature of the cell so molecules move faster
It adds energy to the products so that they form more quickly
It increases the overall energy released by the whole of the reaction
questions.explanation: Enzymes provide an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more substrate molecules can react at body temperature. The overall energy change between reactants and products stays the same.

questions.stem: Why does the enzyme sucrase break down sucrose but not starch?
options: Starch is a protein, and sucrase acts only on carbohydrate molecules
Its active site is complementary in shape only to sucrose molecules
Starch is too small to bind to the active site of the sucrase enzyme
Sucrase is used up after it breaks down its first sucrose molecule
questions.explanation: Enzymes are specific because each active site fits only substrates of a particular shape and chemistry. Starch is a large carbohydrate polymer, not a protein, and enzymes are reused.

questions.stem: Why are enzymes essential to cells?
options: Without them, cells would have no source of energy because enzymes are broken down for ATP
Without them, cells could not take in water, because enzymes form the channels in membranes
Without them, cells would have no DNA, because enzymes carry the cell's genetic information
Without them, most cell reactions would be far too slow at body temperature to sustain life
questions.explanation: Enzymes allow reactions such as respiration, digestion and synthesis to happen quickly at around 37°C. Raising body temperature enough to speed reactions without enzymes would denature proteins.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the lock and key model of enzyme action?
options: The substrate fits exactly into a rigid active site, as a key fits a lock
The active site changes shape around the substrate as it binds to it
The substrate changes the enzyme into a new molecule that is the product
The enzyme fits inside the substrate, as a lock fits around its key
questions.explanation: In the lock and key model the active site has a fixed shape complementary to the substrate. A change of shape on binding is the induced fit model.

questions.stem: How does the induced fit model differ from the lock and key model?
options: The enzyme binds many unrelated substrates because its active site has no shape
The enzyme is used up as it moulds itself around the substrate molecule
The active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, giving a closer fit
The substrate changes shape permanently so that it can fit any active site
questions.explanation: In the induced fit model the active site is flexible and moulds around the substrate, which can strain the substrate's bonds and help the reaction. The enzyme returns to its original shape after the products are released.

questions.stem: Some enzymes can act on a small group of similar substrates, and X-ray studies show their active sites change shape when a substrate binds. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The evidence shows enzymes are not specific, so neither model can be correct
The evidence shows the substrate binds outside the active site of the enzyme
The evidence supports the induced fit model better than the lock and key model
The evidence supports the lock and key model, because each enzyme has an exact fit
questions.explanation: A flexible active site that changes shape on binding, and that can accommodate several similar molecules, is what the induced fit model predicts. A rigid lock and key fit would allow only one exact substrate.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of the lock and key model?
options: It suggests the enzyme is reused, but enzymes are always used up in the reaction
It shows the active site as a pocket, but enzymes actually have no active site
It treats the active site as rigid, but active sites change shape when substrates bind
It suggests enzymes are specific, but enzymes can actually catalyse any reaction
questions.explanation: The lock and key model explains specificity well but shows a fixed active site. Evidence that active sites are flexible led to the induced fit model. Enzymes really are specific and reusable.

questions.stem: Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increase as temperature rises from 10°C to 30°C?
options: The enzyme's active site gets larger, so several substrate molecules can bind at once
The enzyme changes into a different enzyme that has a faster rate of reaction
The substrate molecules break apart on their own without needing the enzyme
Molecules gain kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide more often and with more energy
questions.explanation: Higher temperature means faster-moving molecules, so successful collisions between enzyme and substrate become more frequent, up to the optimum. The active site does not grow or change identity.

questions.stem: Samples of an amylase are kept at 5°C or heated at 80°C for 10 minutes. Both are then tested at 37°C. The 5°C sample works normally; the 80°C sample does not work at all. What explains this?
options: Low temperature only slowed the enzyme, but high temperature denatured it permanently
Low temperature denatured the enzyme, but it recovered once it was warmed back up
High temperature used up the enzyme's energy, and it needs time to recharge
Both samples were denatured, but the 5°C sample was protected by the cold water
questions.explanation: Cold reduces molecular movement but does not change the enzyme's shape, so activity returns on warming. Heating well above the optimum breaks the bonds holding the active site's shape, and this denaturation is usually irreversible.

questions.stem: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: Its amino acids are broken apart and absorbed by the cell for building new proteins
Its active site is blocked by a molecule of product that cannot be released again
It is converted into a different substrate, which another enzyme then breaks down further
The bonds holding its three-dimensional shape break, so the active site changes shape
questions.explanation: Denaturation disrupts the hydrogen bonds and other interactions that hold a protein's folded shape, so the substrate no longer fits the active site. The chain of amino acids itself is not broken into separate amino acids.

questions.stem: Pepsin works best at about pH 2 in the stomach and trypsin works best at about pH 8 in the small intestine. A protein solution is buffered at pH 2. Which result is expected?
options: Pepsin digests the protein, but trypsin shows little or no activity
Trypsin digests the protein, but pepsin shows little or no activity
Both enzymes digest the protein at the same rate at this pH
Neither enzyme works, because proteins cannot be digested in acid
questions.explanation: Each enzyme has an optimum pH matching where it works in the body. At pH 2 pepsin is near its optimum, while trypsin is far from its optimum and largely inactive.

questions.stem: Why does moving an enzyme away from its optimum pH reduce its activity?
options: Changing pH makes the enzyme dissolve, so it can no longer move through the solution
Changing H⁺ concentration alters charges on amino acids, changing the active site's shape
Changing pH changes the temperature of the solution, so the molecules move more slowly
Changing pH breaks the substrate molecules apart, so there is nothing left for the enzyme to bind
questions.explanation: The shape of the active site depends on attractions between charged and polar amino acids. Extra or fewer hydrogen ions change those charges, so the active site loses its shape and the substrate binds less well.

questions.stem: In a catalase experiment, the rate of oxygen production has levelled off at a high hydrogen peroxide concentration. Adding more catalase then increases the rate. What was limiting the rate before the catalase was added?
options: The temperature of the reaction mixture
The volume of oxygen already produced
The number of enzyme active sites available
The concentration of hydrogen peroxide
questions.explanation: At the plateau every active site is occupied, so extra substrate cannot raise the rate; enzyme concentration is limiting. Adding more enzyme provides more active sites, so the rate rises again.

questions.stem: On a graph of reaction rate against substrate concentration, the rate rises steeply at low substrate concentrations. What limits the rate in this part of the graph?
options: The pH, because the substrate changes the acidity of the solution
The substrate concentration, because many active sites are free
The enzyme concentration, because all of the active sites are full
The temperature, because the enzyme is close to being denatured
questions.explanation: At low substrate concentrations, active sites are often empty, so adding substrate increases how often enzyme-substrate complexes form. Only at the plateau does enzyme concentration become limiting.

questions.stem: Students compare catalase activity in potato at different temperatures by adding potato discs to hydrogen peroxide. Which method gives the most precise measure of the rate?
options: Touching the tubes to see which one feels warmest after five minutes
Collecting the oxygen in a gas syringe and recording its volume every 10 seconds
Watching the bubbles and deciding by eye which tube looks the most active
Smelling the tubes to judge which one is producing the most oxygen gas
questions.explanation: A gas syringe gives a numerical volume of oxygen at set times, from which a rate can be calculated. Judging bubbling by eye is subjective, and oxygen has no smell.

questions.stem: Catalase in a potato extract released 30 mL of oxygen in the first 75 seconds. What was the mean rate of oxygen production?
options: 0.4 mL/s
2.5 mL/s
4.0 mL/s
questions.explanation: Rate = volume ÷ time = 30 mL ÷ 75 s = 0.4 mL/s. Dividing time by volume (75 ÷ 30) gives 2.5, which has the units the wrong way around.

questions.stem: Times for amylase to break down all the starch were: pH 4, 300 s; pH 5, 120 s; pH 6, 60 s; pH 7, 50 s; pH 8, 150 s. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The optimum is near pH 7, because the starch was broken down fastest there
The optimum is near pH 4, because the reaction ran for the longest time there
Activity rises steadily with pH, because each pH value tested gave a faster rate
pH has no effect, because starch was broken down at every pH that was tested
questions.explanation: The shortest time means the fastest rate (rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time), so activity peaks near pH 7 and falls on either side. The longest time shows the slowest rate, not the optimum.

questions.stem: An enzyme from bacteria living in a hot spring has an optimum of about 75°C. How would it most likely behave at 37°C?
options: It would not work at all, because the substrate would freeze
It would work slowly, but it would not be denatured
It would be denatured, because 37°C is below its optimum
It would work faster than at 75°C, because cooler is safer
questions.explanation: Below the optimum, molecules collide less often, so the rate is lower, but the enzyme's shape is intact. Denaturation is caused by temperatures above the optimum, not below it.

questions.stem: On a graph of enzyme activity against temperature, activity rises gradually to the optimum and then falls much more steeply. Why is the fall steeper than the rise?
options: Above the optimum, the substrate is used up, so there is nothing left for the enzyme to act on
Above the optimum, molecules move more slowly, so collisions become rapidly less frequent
Above the optimum, the enzyme makes new active sites, which then block one another
Above the optimum, denaturation rapidly destroys active sites, outweighing faster collisions
questions.explanation: Below the optimum, rate rises steadily with collision frequency. Above it, more enzyme molecules denature with each degree, so the number of working active sites falls sharply, even though molecules move faster.
